newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Cash shortage threatens Serbia's spring sowing.
newsitem.headline: Cash shortage threatens Serbia's spring sowing.

text.p: A lack of government funds is seriously threatening Serbia's optimistic spring sowing programme to plant some 2.3 million hectares of arable land, experts said on Thursday.
"Farmers tell us not to send them ministers and other government officials but someone who has the money," Zaharije Trnavcevic, chairman of the agricultural committee in the Serbian parliament, said.
"Spring sowing is completely uncertain as the farmers have not been paid yet for last year's crops," he told Reuters.
Farmers threatened earlier to boycott spring planting unless they got what was owed to them.
The government's 1996 debt to farmers totalled 800 million dinars out of which 425.5 million was owed for sugar beet, 267 million for sunflowers and the rest for tobacco and grapes.
Serbia intended to clear its late payments partly in cash and partly in exchange for fuel and fertilisers and set March 15 as the deadline for paying its sugar beet and sunflower debts.
"But only 35.8 million dinars in cash was secured by February 24 out of which 23 million is for sugar beet and 12.7 million for sunflower debts," Trnavcevic said.
"That is not enough and the prospects for spring planting are very bleak."
Analysts say farmers from the country's bread-basket region of Vojvodina will have to sow but will have great difficulties and cultivation will not be at an adequate level.
"The acreage sown will be well below the plan and productivity will be affected too," said one industry expert who asked not to be named.

The government has set an ambitious plan to sow some 1.4 million hectares with maize, 100,000 with sugar beet, 200,000 with sunflower, 80,000 with soy, 255,000 with vegetables and 190,000 with fodder crops this spring.

To cultivate the land and succesfully carry out the campaign, the government must secure 21,000 tonnes of seeds, 1.1 million tonnes of fertilisers, 10,000 tonnes of herbicides and about 100,000 tonnes of fuel.
A government source claimed all the needed quantities were secured, but a Serbian chamber of commerce official said the government was preparing an urgent import of fertilisers.

"The government is in the process of importing 30,000 tonnes of fertilisers to meet the outstanding needs ahead of the spring sowing," said Bogdan Obradovic, secretary of the agricultural board in the chamber.
Besides lack of funds and a restrictive credit policy, outdated agricultural machinery was also a big problem for the farmers, Obradovic added.
"About 400,000 tractors, which are on average about 16 years old, must be overhauled before the start of the campaign."
The cost of the spring campaign was estimated at about three billion dinars, out of which 1.2 billion was for pre-financing.
Yugoslavia expects agricultural production to grow by six percent and exports of agricultural products to reach $420 million this year.
